summary: A phosphene is the perception of light without light entering the eye. It can be caused by mechanical pressure, electrical or magnetic stimulation, radiation, certain medications or diseases, and by random firing in the visual system. The note covers causes, mechanism, anthropological interpretations of Upper Paleolithic art, and research into visual prostheses and the BrainNet brain-to-brain interface.
one_line: Overview of phosphenes, the perception of light without light entering the eye, covering their causes, mechanisms, anthropological significance and use in visual prostheses and brain-to-brain communication research.
key_facts: The word phosphene comes from the Greek words phos (light) and phainein (to show).
Pressure phosphenes, the most common type, are caused by rubbing or pressing on or near the closed eyes; they were known since antiquity and described by the Greeks.
Isaac Newton described pressing the side of the eye and seeing a colored ring of light on the opposite side.
The name 'phosphene' was coined by J. B. H. Savigny, the ship's surgeon of the wrecked French frigate Méduse, and was first used by Serre d'Uzes to test retinal function before cataract surgery.
Otfrid Foerster reported phosphenes from electrical stimulation of the brain as early as 1929.

Brindley and Lewin (1968) implanted a matrix of electrodes into the visual cortex of a 52-year-old blind female, producing points, spots and bars of light; Brindley and Rushton (1974) used phosphenes to depict Braille spots in a visual prosthesis.
When the visual cortex is stimulated above the calcarine fissure, phosphenes appear in the lower part of the visual field, and vice versa.
Astronauts exposed to radiation in space have reported phosphenes, and radiotherapy patients have reported blue flashes resembling Cherenkov radiation.

Most vision researchers believe phosphenes result from normal visual system activity triggered by a non-light stimulus; Grüsser et al. showed that eye pressure activates retinal ganglion cells similarly to light.
In 1988, David Lewis-Williams and T. A. Dowson argued that non-figurative Upper Paleolithic art depicts phosphenes and neurological 'form constants', probably enhanced by hallucinogenic drugs.
Visual prosthesis research using electrodes implanted over the occipital lobe has been hindered by risks such as infections and seizures.

In the BrainNet experiment, 5 groups of three people (two senders using EEG, one receiver wearing a TMS helmet) played a Tetris-style game; icons flashing at 15 Hz and 17 Hz signaled rotation direction, and the experiment achieved 81% success.
